angle: the 4% rule in 20 lessons, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: The 4% Rule: How Much You Need to Never Work Again

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. How much money do you need to never work again? Most people have no idea. They guess a number like one million or five million and hope it's enough. But there's a simple rule of thumb that gives you a real starting point in about five seconds. It's called the four percent rule. Today I'll show you how it works, where it came from, where it breaks, and how to use it to build your own freedom number.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the rule. Take what you spend in a year and multiply it by twenty five. If you spend forty thousand dollars a year, your target is one million dollars. Why twenty five? Because four percent of one million is forty thousand. The idea is that you could withdraw about four percent in your first year of retirement, adjust for inflation after that, and have a good chance of your money lasting around thirty years.

card.note: a rule of thumb from historical U.S. data, not a guarantee

scenes.short_hook: Multiply your yearly spending by twenty five. That's your freedom number.

scenes.text: That simple multiplication changes how people think about retirement. Suddenly, freedom isn't a vague dream. It's a number tied directly to your lifestyle. And it reveals something powerful. Lowering your spending doesn't just help you save more. It also lowers the number you need. Every one thousand dollars you cut from yearly spending reduces your target by about twenty five thousand dollars.
scenes.caption: SPEND LESS, NEED LESS

scenes.text: We'll look at the four percent rule from three angles. First, the numbers. Where the rule came from, what it assumes and how risky it really is. Second, the psychology. Why spending your savings is so hard, and why so many people get the number wrong. And third, the playbook. How to calculate your own number, reach it and make it last. Reminder, this is education, not financial advice, and nothing about the future is guaranteed.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And first, where did this rule actually come from?
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers. The four percent rule comes from William Bengen's 1994 study in the Journal of Financial Planning, and was supported by the 1998 Trinity study by Philip Cooley, Carl Hubbard and Daniel Walz. Recent safe withdrawal research comes from Morningstar. Social Security figures come from the Social Security Administration. Growth examples use stated average returns, as illustrations, not promises.
scenes.caption: OUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven lessons about what the four percent rule really says, and what it doesn't.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number one. Where the four percent rule came from.
scenes.caption: LESSON 1

scenes.text: In 1994, a financial planner named William Bengen asked a simple question. How much can a retiree withdraw from savings each year without running out of money? He tested historical U.S. market data going back to 1926, imagining retirees starting in every possible year.
scenes.caption: BENGEN, 1994

scenes.text: He assumed a portfolio split between stocks and intermediate term government bonds. The retiree withdrew a set percentage in year one, then increased the dollar amount each year with inflation, no matter what markets did.
scenes.caption: STOCKS AND BONDS

scenes.text: His finding was that a first year withdrawal of about four percent, adjusted for inflation afterward, lasted at least thirty years in every historical period he tested, including retirements that began just before the Great Depression and the high inflation of the 1970s.
scenes.caption: LASTED 30 YEARS IN EVERY PERIOD

scenes.text: Four years later, three professors at Trinity University published a similar study, often called the Trinity study. It also found that withdrawal rates around four percent had high historical success rates over thirty years for portfolios with a large share of stocks.
scenes.caption: THE TRINITY STUDY

scenes.text: Bengen himself later suggested that with more asset classes, slightly higher starting rates might have worked historically. But four percent stuck, because it's simple and memorable. It became one of the most famous rules in personal finance.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE AND MEMORABLE

scenes.text: Lesson number two. Turn your spending into a target.
scenes.caption: LESSON 2

scenes.text: The flip side of a four percent withdrawal is the times twenty five rule. If four percent of your portfolio covers one year of spending, then you need twenty five years of spending saved. Spend thirty thousand a year, you need about seven hundred fifty thousand. Spend sixty thousand, you need about one point five million.
scenes.caption: $30K NEEDS $750K, $60K NEEDS $1.5M

scenes.text: Notice that this uses spending, not income. Someone earning two hundred thousand dollars but spending one hundred eighty thousand needs four and a half million dollars. Someone earning sixty thousand but spending thirty thousand needs only seven hundred fifty thousand. Your lifestyle sets your target.
scenes.caption: SPENDING SETS THE TARGET

scenes.text: It's also about spending in retirement, which may differ from today. Some costs disappear, like commuting or a mortgage that's paid off. Others may rise, like health care and travel.
scenes.caption: RETIREMENT SPENDING CHANGES

scenes.text: And the money that counts is the money coming from your portfolio. Income from Social Security, a pension or part time work reduces how much you need to withdraw, and therefore how much you need saved.
scenes.caption: OTHER INCOME LOWERS THE TARGET

scenes.text: Try this. Add up your yearly spending, subtract any guaranteed retirement income you expect, and multiply what's left by twenty five. That's your first draft freedom number.
scenes.caption: YOUR FIRST DRAFT NUMBER

scenes.text: Lesson number three. The order of returns matters.

card.title: Sequence of returns risk
card.sub: bad timing can sink a plan

scenes.caption: LESSON 3

scenes.text: When you're saving, the order of good and bad years doesn't change your final result much if you just hold. But when you're withdrawing, it matters enormously. This is called sequence of returns risk.
scenes.caption: SEQUENCE RISK
scenes.short_hook: Two retirees. Same returns. One ends up with far less. Here's why.

scenes.text: Here's an illustration. Two retirees each start with one million dollars and withdraw forty thousand a year. Both experience exactly the same twelve yearly returns, just in a different order. For one, the two bad years come first. For the other, they come last.
scenes.caption: SAME RETURNS, DIFFERENT ORDER

scenes.text: After twelve years, the retiree who faced the bad years first has roughly seven hundred forty thousand dollars left. The one who faced them last has roughly one million. Same average, very different result, because selling investments to fund withdrawals after a crash locks in losses.
scenes.caption: $740K VS $1M

scenes.text: This is why the first five to ten years of retirement are often called the danger zone. A big crash early on can do lasting damage to a portfolio that's also funding withdrawals.
scenes.caption: THE DANGER ZONE

scenes.text: Many retirees manage this risk by holding a few years of spending in bonds or cash, so they don't have to sell stocks during a downturn, and by being willing to cut spending a little in bad years.
scenes.caption: A CASH BUFFER HELPS

scenes.text: Lesson number four. Four percent isn't a guarantee.
scenes.caption: LESSON 4

scenes.text: The four percent rule is based on U.S. history. It worked in every historical thirty year period Bengen tested, but there's no promise the future will look like the past. Future returns could be higher or lower.
scenes.caption: HISTORY ISN'T A PROMISE

scenes.text: Some researchers have argued that future returns may be lower than historical averages, which would make four percent riskier. Morningstar's recent research, for example, has estimated a safe starting withdrawal rate for new retirees in the high three percent range, depending on assumptions.
scenes.caption: SOME SUGGEST LOWER RATES

scenes.text: Others point out that in most historical periods, a four percent withdrawal left retirees with much more money than they started with. The rule was designed around the worst cases, so in typical cases it may be conservative.
scenes.caption: OFTEN CONSERVATIVE

scenes.text: The truth is that four percent is a reasonable starting point, not a precise answer. Think of it as a guide for planning, not a law of physics.
scenes.caption: A GUIDE, NOT A LAW

scenes.text: Try this. Run your numbers at both three and a half and four percent. If you'd be comfortable at either, you have a margin of safety.
scenes.caption: TEST 3.5% AND 4%

scenes.text: Lesson number five. The rule assumes about thirty years.
scenes.caption: LESSON 5

scenes.text: Bengen's research focused on retirements lasting around thirty years, which fits someone retiring around sixty five. But someone retiring at forty might need their money to last fifty years or more.
scenes.caption: 30 YEARS VS 50 YEARS

scenes.text: Longer retirements generally require lower withdrawal rates. Many early retirement planners use three to three and a half percent for very long horizons, which means saving roughly twenty nine to thirty three times yearly spending instead of twenty five.
scenes.caption: EARLY RETIREES OFTEN USE 3 TO 3.5%

scenes.text: Life expectancy matters too. Many people live into their nineties, especially couples, where at least one partner often lives a long time. Planning only to age eighty five could leave you short.
scenes.caption: PLAN FOR A LONG LIFE

scenes.text: On the other hand, someone retiring at seventy may be able to withdraw a bit more, because their money doesn't need to last as long.
scenes.caption: LATER RETIREMENT, HIGHER RATE

scenes.text: Try this. Decide how many years your money needs to last, from your planned retirement age to at least ninety five, and adjust your withdrawal rate to match.
scenes.caption: PLAN TO 95

scenes.text: Lesson number six. Your investment mix matters.
scenes.caption: LESSON 6

scenes.text: The four percent rule assumed a meaningful share of stocks, often fifty to seventy five percent. Stocks provide growth that helps your money keep up with inflation over decades.
scenes.caption: STOCKS PROVIDE GROWTH

scenes.text: Many people assume retirement money should be entirely in safe investments. But a portfolio that's too conservative may not grow fast enough to support inflation adjusted withdrawals for thirty years. In Bengen's research, very low stock allocations had lower safe withdrawal rates.
scenes.caption: TOO SAFE CAN BE RISKY

scenes.text: Bonds and cash still play an important role. They reduce volatility and provide money to spend during stock market downturns, helping with sequence risk.
scenes.caption: BONDS REDUCE SWINGS

scenes.text: The right mix depends on your age, other income and comfort with ups and downs. Target date funds and balanced funds offer simple ready made mixes.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE READY MADE MIXES

scenes.text: Try this. Look at your current mix of stocks and bonds and ask whether it fits your timeline. If you're decades from retirement, a very conservative mix may be holding you back.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR MIX

scenes.text: Lesson number seven. Don't forget inflation and taxes.
scenes.caption: LESSON 7

scenes.text: The four percent rule raises your withdrawals with inflation each year, which is crucial. At three percent inflation, prices roughly double in about twenty four years. Forty thousand dollars of spending today could mean around eighty thousand later in retirement.
scenes.caption: PRICES CAN DOUBLE

scenes.text: Taxes are another factor. The rule is typically calculated before taxes. Withdrawals from traditional four oh one ks and IRAs are usually taxed as income, while qualified Roth withdrawals are tax free and taxable accounts may face capital gains taxes.
scenes.caption: WITHDRAWALS MAY BE TAXED

scenes.text: So if you need forty thousand dollars a year to spend, you may need to withdraw more than that from pre tax accounts to cover taxes. Your freedom number should account for this.
scenes.caption: PLAN FOR TAXES

scenes.text: Having money in different types of accounts, pre tax, Roth and taxable, can give you flexibility to manage taxes in retirement.
scenes.caption: TAX FLEXIBILITY

scenes.text: Try this. Estimate how much of your retirement savings is in pre tax accounts, and add a cushion to your freedom number for taxes.
scenes.caption: ADD A TAX CUSHION

scenes.text: That's angle one. Where the rule came from, the times twenty five rule, sequence risk, no guarantees, time horizon, investment mix, and inflation and taxes. Now angle two. The psychology.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The math of retirement is only half the challenge. The other half is emotional. Saving for decades and then spending your savings feels very different from what most people expect. Here are seven psychological lessons about the four percent rule.
scenes.caption: THE EMOTIONAL HALF

scenes.text: Lesson number eight. A number turns a dream into a plan.

card.title: The number makes it real
card.sub: a vague goal becomes a target

scenes.caption: LESSON 8

scenes.text: Most people approach retirement with vague hopes. Someday, enough, comfortable. Without a number, it's hard to know whether you're on track, so many people either worry constantly or ignore it entirely.
scenes.caption: VAGUE GOALS CREATE ANXIETY

scenes.text: The four percent rule gives you a concrete target. Once you know you need, say, one point two million dollars, you can calculate how much to save each month and track your progress.
scenes.caption: A CONCRETE TARGET

scenes.text: Research on goal setting, including work by psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham, has found that specific, challenging goals tend to lead to better performance than vague goals like do your best.
scenes.caption: SPECIFIC GOALS WORK BETTER

scenes.text: Tracking progress toward your number can be motivating. Watching yourself move from ten percent to twenty five percent to fifty percent of the way there makes the journey feel real.
scenes.caption: TRACK YOUR PERCENTAGE

scenes.text: Try this. Calculate what percentage of your freedom number you have today. Write it down and check it once a year.
scenes.caption: WHAT PERCENT ARE YOU?

scenes.text: Lesson number nine. Spending savings is surprisingly hard.
scenes.caption: LESSON 9

scenes.text: After decades of saving, many retirees find it emotionally difficult to start spending. Watching a balance go down can feel like failure, even when it's exactly the plan.
scenes.caption: SPENDING FEELS LIKE FAILURE
scenes.short_hook: Many retirees are scared to spend money they spent decades saving.

scenes.text: Research by the Employee Benefit Research Institute and others has found that many retirees spend down their savings slowly, and some keep much of their savings intact well into retirement, often out of caution and uncertainty.
scenes.caption: MANY UNDERSPEND

scenes.text: Caution can be wise, but underspending has a cost too. Money saved for decades might never be used for the experiences and security it was meant to provide.
scenes.caption: UNDERSPENDING HAS A COST

scenes.text: A clear withdrawal plan, like the four percent rule, can actually make spending easier. It gives you permission to spend a set amount with confidence.
scenes.caption: A PLAN GIVES PERMISSION

scenes.text: Try this. If you're retired or close, write down what a safe yearly spending amount looks like for you, and give yourself permission to use it.
scenes.caption: GIVE YOURSELF PERMISSION

scenes.text: Lesson number ten. Lifestyle creep moves the finish line.
scenes.caption: LESSON 10

scenes.text: As income grows, spending often grows with it. Bigger house, nicer car, more expensive vacations. Each upgrade feels small, but together they raise your yearly spending.
scenes.caption: SPENDING GROWS WITH INCOME

scenes.text: Because of the times twenty five rule, every permanent ten thousand dollar increase in yearly spending raises your freedom number by about two hundred fifty thousand dollars. Lifestyle creep doesn't just reduce what you save. It moves the finish line further away.
scenes.caption: $10K MORE SPENDING, $250K MORE NEEDED

scenes.text: The opposite is also true. Reducing yearly spending by ten thousand dollars lowers the target by about two hundred fifty thousand, and frees up money to save. It's a double benefit.
scenes.caption: THE DOUBLE BENEFIT

scenes.text: This doesn't mean never upgrading your life. It means making upgrades deliberately, knowing what each one costs in years of work.
scenes.caption: UPGRADE DELIBERATELY

scenes.text: Try this. Before any big recurring expense, multiply its yearly cost by twenty five. That's what it adds to your freedom number.
scenes.caption: MULTIPLY BY 25

scenes.text: Quick pause. If knowing your freedom number sounds useful, please subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free, and it helps us keep making these. Now, lesson eleven.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number eleven. One more year syndrome.
scenes.caption: LESSON 11

scenes.text: Many people reach their number and still don't stop working. They think, just one more year, to be safe. Then another. And another. The finish line keeps moving because fear keeps moving it.
scenes.caption: JUST ONE MORE YEAR

scenes.text: Some extra cushion can be smart, especially with uncertain markets. But years are the one resource you can't get back. Working years longer than necessary trades healthy, active years for money you may never need.
scenes.caption: YEARS ARE PRICELESS

scenes.text: A plan with flexibility, like being willing to cut spending in bad years or earn some part time income, can give you the confidence to stop when you've reached a reasonable target.
scenes.caption: FLEXIBILITY BUILDS CONFIDENCE

scenes.text: It also helps to think about what you're retiring to, not just from. People with clear plans for their time often feel more ready to make the leap.
scenes.caption: RETIRE TO SOMETHING

scenes.text: Try this. Write down what would make you feel ready to stop full time work. A number, a buffer, a plan for your days. Then hold yourself to it.
scenes.caption: DEFINE READY

scenes.text: Lesson number twelve. Financial freedom doesn't have to mean stopping work.
scenes.caption: LESSON 12

scenes.text: Many people who reach financial independence keep working, but on their own terms. Part time, a passion project, a lower stress job or starting a business. The freedom is in the choice.
scenes.caption: FREEDOM IS CHOICE

scenes.text: Even partial financial independence is powerful. If your savings could cover half your spending, you could take a lower paying job you love, or work fewer hours.
scenes.caption: PARTIAL FREEDOM COUNTS

scenes.text: Some people use the idea of coast FIRE, where they've saved enough that their investments could grow to their full number by traditional retirement age, even without more contributions. From there, they only need to cover current expenses.
scenes.caption: COAST FIRE

scenes.text: Earning even a small income in early retirement can dramatically reduce how much you need to withdraw, making your money last much longer.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE INCOME GOES FAR

scenes.text: Try this. Calculate what percentage of your spending your savings could cover today using four percent. That's your current level of freedom.
scenes.caption: YOUR FREEDOM LEVEL

scenes.text: Lesson number thirteen. Define enough for yourself.
scenes.caption: LESSON 13

scenes.text: Some people chase five or ten million because that's what wealthy people seem to have. But your freedom number depends only on your own spending, not anyone else's.
scenes.query: Mountain of money versus modest home
scenes.caption: YOUR NUMBER, NOT THEIRS

scenes.text: Morgan Housel writes that one of the hardest financial skills is getting the goalpost to stop moving. Without a sense of enough, no amount ever feels sufficient.
scenes.caption: STOP MOVING THE GOALPOST

scenes.text: A clear number tied to a lifestyle you actually want can bring peace. You know what you're working toward, and you know when you've arrived.
scenes.caption: ENOUGH BRINGS PEACE

scenes.text: That doesn't mean you can't want more. It means the more is a choice, not a requirement for feeling secure.
scenes.caption: MORE IS A CHOICE

scenes.text: Try this. Describe your ideal ordinary week in retirement, then estimate what it costs. That's the foundation of your enough.
scenes.caption: DESCRIBE YOUR IDEAL WEEK

scenes.text: Lesson number fourteen. Flexible plans beat rigid ones.
scenes.caption: LESSON 14

scenes.text: The original four percent rule assumes you raise withdrawals with inflation every year, no matter what. Real people don't usually behave that rigidly. They cut back in bad years and spend more in good ones.
scenes.caption: REAL PEOPLE ADJUST

scenes.text: Research on flexible withdrawal strategies, such as guardrail approaches developed by planners Jonathan Guyton and William Klinger, suggests that being willing to trim spending after poor markets can support higher starting withdrawal rates.
scenes.caption: GUARDRAILS

scenes.text: Flexibility reduces anxiety. If you know you'd cut travel for a year or two during a crash, a bad market feels less like a threat to your entire retirement.
scenes.caption: FLEXIBILITY REDUCES FEAR

scenes.text: Separating spending into needs and wants helps. Cover essential needs with stable income and safer assets, and fund wants from the riskier portfolio.
scenes.caption: NEEDS VERSUS WANTS

scenes.text: Try this. List which retirement expenses you could reduce for a year if markets fell sharply. That list is your safety valve.
scenes.caption: YOUR SAFETY VALVE

scenes.text: That's angle two. The number makes it real, fear of spending, lifestyle creep, one more year, freedom without full retirement, defining enough and flexibility. Now angle three. The playbook.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Let's turn the four percent rule into a practical plan. Six moves to calculate your number, reach it and make it last.
scenes.caption: SIX MOVES

scenes.text: Move number fifteen. Track your real spending.
scenes.caption: LESSON 15

scenes.text: Your freedom number is only as good as your spending estimate. Many people underestimate what they spend by a lot, because small purchases and irregular expenses add up.
scenes.caption: MOST PEOPLE UNDERESTIMATE

scenes.text: Look at at least three to six months of bank and credit card statements, plus yearly expenses like insurance, gifts, car repairs and holidays.
scenes.caption: USE REAL STATEMENTS

scenes.text: Then estimate how spending will change in retirement. Remove work costs and add things like health insurance before Medicare, which generally starts at sixty five.
scenes.caption: ADJUST FOR RETIREMENT

scenes.text: Budgeting apps or a simple spreadsheet can help. The goal isn't perfection, just a realistic number. Many people find it helpful to sort spending into three groups, essentials like housing and food, regular extras like dining out, and one time costs like a new roof. Each group behaves differently in retirement.
scenes.caption: REALISTIC, NOT PERFECT

scenes.text: Try this. Add up last year's total spending from your statements. It might surprise you.
scenes.caption: ADD UP LAST YEAR

scenes.text: Move number sixteen. Calculate your freedom number.
scenes.caption: LESSON 16

scenes.text: Start with expected yearly retirement spending. Subtract guaranteed income, like Social Security or a pension. Multiply what's left by twenty five, or by twenty nine to thirty three for very long early retirements.
scenes.caption: THE FORMULA

scenes.text: Example. Spending of sixty thousand dollars, minus twenty four thousand from Social Security, leaves thirty six thousand to come from investments. Times twenty five equals nine hundred thousand dollars.
scenes.caption: $36K TIMES 25 = $900K

scenes.text: Add a cushion for taxes if much of your money is in pre tax accounts, and consider a buffer for big future costs like home repairs or helping family.
scenes.caption: ADD CUSHIONS

scenes.text: Revisit your number every few years. Your life, spending and the economy will change.
scenes.caption: REVISIT IT

scenes.text: Try this. Do the calculation today and write your freedom number somewhere you'll see it.
scenes.caption: WRITE YOUR NUMBER

scenes.text: Move number seventeen. Factor in Social Security.
scenes.caption: LESSON 17

scenes.text: Social Security is an inflation adjusted income stream for life, something very valuable. In 2025, the average retired worker benefit was around two thousand dollars a month, according to the Social Security Administration.
scenes.caption: AROUND $2,000 A MONTH ON AVERAGE
scenes.short_hook: Social Security can cut the amount you need to save by hundreds of thousands.

scenes.text: Twenty four thousand dollars a year of Social Security would otherwise require about six hundred thousand dollars of savings under the four percent rule. That's a big reduction in what you need to save.
scenes.caption: WORTH ABOUT $600K OF SAVINGS

scenes.text: When you claim matters. Claiming before full retirement age reduces benefits, while waiting past it, up to age seventy, increases them. For many people, delaying can significantly boost lifetime income.
scenes.caption: WHEN YOU CLAIM MATTERS

scenes.text: You can see your estimated benefits by creating an account on the Social Security Administration's website. Your statement shows estimates at different claiming ages, so you can see exactly how much waiting could add to your monthly check, and how that changes the amount you need to save.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR ESTIMATE

scenes.text: Try this. Log in to your Social Security account, check your estimated benefit and subtract it from your retirement spending before calculating your number.
scenes.caption: SUBTRACT IT

scenes.text: Move number eighteen. Build a plan to reach your number.

card.title: Close the gap
card.sub: how fast you can get there

scenes.caption: LESSON 18

scenes.text: Once you know your number, you can estimate how long it'll take. At a seven percent average yearly return, investing one thousand dollars a month could reach one million dollars in roughly twenty seven to twenty eight years, starting from zero.
scenes.caption: $1,000 A MONTH: ABOUT 28 YEARS

scenes.text: Two thousand dollars a month could get there in roughly twenty years. Three thousand a month, in roughly fifteen and a half years. Your savings rate is one of the biggest levers you control.
scenes.caption: $2,000: 20 YEARS, $3,000: 15.5

scenes.text: Raising income, cutting big expenses and investing raises are the most powerful ways to speed things up. The big three expenses for most households are housing, transportation and food. Small wins there can shave years off your timeline, far more than skipping the occasional coffee.
scenes.caption: THREE BIG LEVERS

scenes.text: Use tax advantaged accounts first, like four oh one ks, IRAs and HSAs, so more of your money compounds.
scenes.caption: TAX ADVANTAGED FIRST

scenes.text: Try this. Use an online compound interest calculator with your current savings, monthly amount and seven percent to see your estimated timeline.
scenes.caption: SEE YOUR TIMELINE

scenes.text: Move number nineteen. Protect the first years of retirement.
scenes.caption: LESSON 19

scenes.text: Because sequence risk is greatest early on, many retirees hold one to three years of spending in cash or short term bonds when they retire. If markets crash, they spend from that buffer instead of selling stocks low.
scenes.caption: A 1 TO 3 YEAR BUFFER

scenes.text: Some people use a bucket strategy. Near term money in cash, medium term money in bonds and long term money in stocks.
scenes.caption: THE BUCKET STRATEGY

scenes.text: Others reduce their stock allocation around retirement and gradually increase it again later, an approach some researchers have studied as a way to manage sequence risk.
scenes.caption: ADJUST YOUR MIX

scenes.text: Having part time income or flexibility in the first few years can also protect your portfolio enormously. Even ten or fifteen thousand dollars a year from consulting or a part time job means you withdraw less during the years when a crash would hurt the most.
scenes.caption: EARLY FLEXIBILITY

scenes.text: Try this. If you're within five years of retirement, plan how you'd cover two years of spending without selling stocks.
scenes.caption: PLAN TWO YEARS

scenes.text: Move number twenty. Review and adjust every year.

card.title: Review and adjust
card.sub: the rule is a starting point

scenes.caption: LESSON 20

scenes.text: The four percent rule is a starting point, not autopilot. Each year in retirement, review your portfolio, spending and the market.
scenes.caption: REVIEW EVERY YEAR

scenes.text: If your portfolio has grown a lot, you may be able to spend more. If it has fallen sharply, a small temporary cut can help protect your plan.
scenes.caption: ADJUST AS NEEDED

scenes.text: Many retirees work with a fee only fiduciary financial planner for these decisions, especially around taxes, Social Security and withdrawals.
scenes.caption: GET HELP IF NEEDED

scenes.text: The goal isn't to follow a rule perfectly. It's to spend confidently while making sure your money lasts. A plan that you review, understand and adjust will serve you far better than any single number followed blindly for thirty years.
scenes.caption: SPEND WITH CONFIDENCE

scenes.text: Try this. Pick an annual review date and write down the questions you'll ask yourself each year.
scenes.caption: PICK A REVIEW DATE

scenes.text: Let's run the four percent rule for three different households, so you can see how much the number depends on lifestyle and other income. These are simplified illustrations, before taxes, just to show how the math works.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Household one is a single person who spends thirty thousand dollars a year, owns a modest paid off condo and expects about twenty thousand dollars a year from Social Security. That leaves ten thousand dollars a year to come from savings. Times twenty five, their freedom number is about two hundred fifty thousand dollars. Far less than the million most people imagine.
scenes.caption: HOUSEHOLD 1: ABOUT $250K

scenes.text: Household two is a couple spending sixty thousand dollars a year, with combined Social Security of about thirty six thousand. They need twenty four thousand a year from savings, so their freedom number is about six hundred thousand dollars. If they downsize their home and cut yearly spending to fifty thousand, the number falls to about three hundred fifty thousand.
scenes.caption: HOUSEHOLD 2: ABOUT $600K

scenes.text: Household three is a family that spends one hundred twenty thousand dollars a year and wants to retire at fifty, long before Social Security begins. For a long retirement they use three and a half percent, so they divide by point zero three five. Their freedom number is roughly three point four million dollars. Lifestyle and timing changed the target enormously.
scenes.caption: HOUSEHOLD 3: ABOUT $3.4M

scenes.text: Same rule, three completely different answers, from a quarter of a million to more than three million dollars. That's why copying someone else's retirement number makes little sense. The only number that matters is the one built from your spending, your income and your timeline.
scenes.caption: YOUR NUMBER IS PERSONAL

scenes.text: In your twenties and thirties, the four percent rule is mostly a motivation tool. Your future spending is uncertain, but knowing that roughly twenty five times spending is the goal helps you see why saving early matters, and why keeping your lifestyle in check gives you options later.
scenes.caption: 20s AND 30s: MOTIVATION
scenes.chapter: Using the rule at every age

scenes.text: In your forties and fifties, the rule becomes a progress check. You have a clearer picture of your spending, your Social Security estimate and your savings. This is the time to compare where you are with where you need to be, and to adjust contributions, catch up savings and your retirement age.
scenes.caption: 40s AND 50s: PROGRESS CHECK

scenes.text: In your sixties and beyond, the rule turns into a spending guide. It helps you decide how much to withdraw each year, when to claim Social Security and how much to keep in safer assets. Many retirees use it as a starting point, then adjust each year with flexibility.
scenes.caption: 60s AND BEYOND: SPENDING GUIDE

scenes.text: Let's put the whole video into a simple five step worksheet you can do tonight with a pen and paper.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Your freedom number in five steps

scenes.text: Step one. Write down what you spend in a typical year, using real bank and credit card statements, not a guess. Include the irregular costs people forget, like car repairs, gifts, annual subscriptions, insurance and holidays. If you're unsure, add ten percent. This number is the foundation for everything else, so it's worth getting right.
scenes.caption: STEP 1: REAL SPENDING

scenes.text: Step two. Adjust that number for retirement. Cross out costs that will likely disappear, like commuting, work clothes, retirement contributions or a mortgage you'll have paid off. Add costs that may appear, like health insurance before Medicare, more travel or helping family. What's left is your estimated retirement spending.
scenes.caption: STEP 2: RETIREMENT SPENDING

scenes.text: Step three. Subtract guaranteed income. Look up your estimated Social Security benefit, and add any pension or reliable rental income. Subtract the yearly total from your retirement spending. The result is the amount your investments need to provide each year.
scenes.caption: STEP 3: SUBTRACT GUARANTEED INCOME

scenes.text: Step four. Multiply. Use twenty five for a traditional thirty year retirement, or around twenty nine to thirty three for a very long early retirement. Then add a cushion if most of your savings are in pre tax accounts, since withdrawals there are usually taxed. That's your freedom number.
scenes.caption: STEP 4: MULTIPLY AND CUSHION

scenes.text: Step five. Compare your freedom number with what you have today, and work out the gap. Then decide how you'll close it, by saving more, earning more, spending less, working a little longer or combining all four. Write the plan next to the number, and revisit both once a year.
scenes.caption: STEP 5: CLOSE THE GAP

scenes.text: Imagine two retirees, each with one million dollars, each planning to withdraw forty thousand dollars a year. In their second year of retirement, the market drops thirty percent. Both portfolios fall sharply, and both feel scared.
scenes.caption: SAME START, SAME CRASH
scenes.short_hook: Two retirees saved the same amount. Only one panicked.

scenes.text: The first retiree panics, sells all their stocks and moves everything to cash. When markets recover over the next few years, their money doesn't. They keep withdrawing forty thousand a year from a shrinking pile, and their plan is now at real risk.
scenes.caption: RETIREE ONE PANICS

scenes.text: The second retiree had a two year cash buffer. They spend from it, trim travel for a year and leave their stocks alone. When markets recover, their portfolio recovers too. Same crash, very different outcomes, because one had a plan for bad years.
scenes.caption: RETIREE TWO HAD A PLAN

scenes.text: The four percent rule didn't save the second retiree by itself. What saved them was the system around it. A realistic number, a cash buffer for bad years, a willingness to adjust spending a little and the discipline to stay invested. The rule tells you where to aim. The system is what gets you through the storms.
scenes.caption: THE SYSTEM MATTERS

scenes.text: Question one. Is four percent too high now? Some researchers suggest slightly lower starting rates for long retirements or lower expected returns. Others think four percent remains reasonable. Using three and a half to four percent with flexibility is a common middle ground.
scenes.caption: IS 4% TOO HIGH?

scenes.text: Question two. Does the rule work for early retirement? It can be a starting point, but longer retirements usually call for lower withdrawal rates, often three to three and a half percent, and more flexibility.
scenes.caption: EARLY RETIREMENT

scenes.text: Question three. What if I have a pension? A pension, like Social Security, reduces how much you need from savings. Subtract it from your spending before multiplying by twenty five.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT PENSIONS?

scenes.text: Question four. Should I include my home's value? Usually not, unless you plan to sell or downsize and use the money for living expenses. Your home provides shelter, not spending money.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT MY HOME?

scenes.text: Question five. What about long term care costs? Long term care can be very expensive, and many retirees will need some help later in life. Some people plan for it with long term care insurance, others set aside extra savings or plan to use home equity. It's worth discussing with a planner, because it can be one of the biggest late life expenses.
scenes.caption: LONG TERM CARE

scenes.text: Question six. Can I retire with less than twenty five times spending? Possibly, with more flexibility. Part time income, delaying Social Security, a willingness to cut spending in bad years, or moving to a lower cost area can all make a smaller number work. The more flexible you are, the less you may need.
scenes.caption: LESS THAN 25 TIMES?

scenes.text: Mistake one. Using income instead of spending. Your freedom number is built from what you spend, not what you earn. Using income can make your target far too high or, if you spend more than you think, far too low.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 1: INCOME, NOT SPENDING

scenes.text: Mistake two. Forgetting health care before Medicare. People who retire before sixty five need health insurance until Medicare starts, and premiums can be significant. Build that cost into your spending estimate.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 2: HEALTH CARE GAP

scenes.text: Mistake three. Treating four percent as guaranteed. It's a historical rule of thumb. Markets, inflation and your lifespan can differ from the past. Build in a margin of safety and stay flexible.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 3: TREATING IT AS A GUARANTEE

scenes.text: Mistake four. Ignoring taxes. Withdrawals from pre tax accounts are usually taxed as income. If you need forty thousand dollars to spend, you may need to withdraw more. Plan for the tax bill.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 4: IGNORING TAXES

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Where the rule came from, the times twenty five rule, sequence risk, no guarantees, time horizon, investment mix, and inflation and taxes.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. A number makes it real, fear of spending, lifestyle creep, one more year, freedom without full retirement, defining enough and flexibility.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Track spending, calculate your number, factor in Social Security, close the gap, protect the early years and review every year.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.text: Your freedom number isn't a fantasy. It's your yearly spending times twenty five, adjusted for your life. Once you know it, you can build a real plan to reach it. If you want my full step by step plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments, what's your freedom number? I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
